questions.q:
A rubber band catapult has initial length $2 \mathrm{~cm}$ and cross-sectional area $5 \mathrm{~mm}^2$. It is stretched to $2 \mathrm{~cm}$ and then released to project a stone of mass of $20 \mathrm{~g}$. The velocity of projected stone is 
(Young's modulus of rubber $=5 \times 10^8 \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}$ )
questions.solution:
According to work-energy theorem, $\mathrm{K} \mathrm{E}$ of stone $=$ Elastic potential energy of rubber band.
Now, for rubber band;
Young's modulus $=5 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}^2$
Length, $L=2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}$
Change of length, $\Delta L=2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}$
Area of cross-section, $A=5 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^2$
Elastic potential energy of rubber band
$\begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{2} \times Y \times(\text { strain })^2 \times \text { volume } \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \times Y \times\left(\frac{\Delta L}{L}\right)^2 \times A \times L \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10^8 \times\left(\frac{2 \times 10^{-2}}{2 \times 10^{-2}}\right)^2 \times 5 \times 10^{-6} \times 2 \times 10^{-2} \\ & =25 \mathrm{~J}\end{aligned}$
This energy is given to stone (mass $=20 \mathrm{~g}$ );
$\Rightarrow \mathrm{KE}$ (stone) = E.P.E (Rubber band)
$\Rightarrow \quad \frac{1}{2} \times m v^2=25\Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 10^{-3} \times v^2=25\begin{array}{ll}\Rightarrow & v^2=\frac{25 \times 2}{20 \times 10^{-3}} \Rightarrow v^2=25 \times 10^2 \\ \Rightarrow & v=5 \times 10=50 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\end{array}$

Now given, $\begin{aligned} L_1 & =3 L_2 \text { and } r_1=3 r_2 \\ \Delta L_1 & =x\end{aligned}$ Also, $\quad F_1=F_2$ So from eq. (i), we have $\frac{3 L_2}{x\left(3 r_2\right)^2}=\frac{L_2}{\Delta L_2 r_2^2} \Rightarrow \Delta L_2=3 x$

questions.q: The length of a rod under longitudinal tension $T_1$ is $L_1$ and that under longitudinal tension $T_2$ is $L_2$. What is the actual length of the rod, in the absence of tensions?

Let, the natural length of wire be $L_0$.
Using Hooke's law,

Y=\frac{T L_0}{A \Delta L}...(i)

where, $Y$ is Young's modulus of elasticity, $T$ is temperature, $A$ is area and $\Delta L$ is change in length, i.e. $\Delta L=L-L_0$

From Eq. (i), we get

L-L_0=\frac{T L_0}{A Y}

Case 1 When tension is $T_1$ and length of wire $L=L_1$,
$L_1-L_0=\frac{T_1 L_0}{A Y}$...(ii)
Case 2 When tension is $T_2$ and length of wire $L=L_2L_2-L_0=\frac{T_2 L_0}{A Y}$...(iii)
Dividing Eq. (ii) by Eq. (iii), we get

\begin{aligned}
& \frac{L_1-L_0}{L_2-L_0}=\frac{T_1}{T_2} \\
\Rightarrow \quad & L_0=\frac{L_1 T_2-L_2 T_1}{T_2-T_1}
\end{aligned}

&

For aluminium wire, \(Y=7 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{Nm}^{-2}\)

\(\therefore \quad r=\frac{d}{2}=\frac{3 \times 10^{-3}}{2} \mathrm{~m}=1.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}\)

\(\Rightarrow \quad \Delta l=\frac{F l}{A Y}=\frac{400 \times 5}{\pi\left(1.5 \times 10^{-3}\right)^2 \times 7 \times 10^{10}}\)
\(\Delta l=\frac{2000}{15.75 \pi \times 10^4}\) ...(ii)
According to given condition, \(\Delta l\) is same in both cases.
From Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get
\(\begin{array}{rlrl}
\therefore & \frac{2000}{12 \pi r^2 \times 10^{10}} & =\frac{2000}{15.75 \pi \times 10^4} \\
\Rightarrow & 12 r^2 & =15.75 \times 10^{-6} \\
r & = & 1.15 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}=1.15 \mathrm{~mm}
\end{array}\)
\(\therefore\) Diameter, \(d=2 r=2 \times 1.15=2.3 \mathrm{~mm}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Assertion (a) : Ductile metals are used to prepare thin wires.Reason (R): In the stress-strain curve of ductile metals, the length between the points representing elastic limit and breaking point is very small.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true. Ductile metals are materials that can be stretched or drawn into thin wires without breaking. This property, known as ductility, is essential for manufacturing wires for applications like electrical wiring and cables. Gold, silver, and copper are examples of highly ductile metals.
Reason (R) is false. The stress-strain curve for a ductile material has a long plastic deformation region between the elastic limit and the breaking point. This is precisely what defines a ductile material-it can undergo significant permanent deformation (plastic deformation) before it fractures. In contrast, a brittle material has a very small or non-existent plastic region, breaking soon after its elastic limit is reached.
The correct option is (3) (A) is true but (R) is false.
